{{Use mdy dates|date=November 2015}}
'''David Robert Morrison''' (born July 29, 1955, in [[Oakland, California]]) is an American mathematician and theoretical physicist. He works on [[string theory]] and [[algebraic geometry]], especially its relations to theoretical physics.

Morrison studied at [[Princeton University]] with bachelor's degree in 1976 and at [[Harvard University]] with master's degree in 1977 and PhD under [[Phillip Griffiths]] in 1980 with thesis ''Semistable Degenerations of Enriques' and Hyperelliptic Surfaces''.<ref name="genealogy">{{MathGenealogy|id=41459|name=David Robert Morrison}}</ref> From 1980 he was an instructor and from 1982 an assistant professor at Princeton University and in the academic year 1984–1985 a visiting scientist at the [[University of Kyoto]] (as Fellow der Japan Society for the Promotion of Science). In 1986 he became an associate professor and in 1992 a professor of mathematics at [[Duke University]] and then in 1997 "James B. Duke Professor of Mathematics and Physics". While at Duke, Morrison advised multiple PhD students, including [[Antonella Grassi]] and [[Carina Curto]].<ref name="genealogy" /><ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Curto|first=Carina|date=2005-05-06|title=Matrix Model Superpotentials and Calabi-Yau Spaces: an ADE Classification|eprint=math/0505111}}</ref> Since 2006 he has been a professor at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]].

Although Morrison began his career as a mathematician in classical algebraic geometry, in his later career he has also been a string theorist. He works on the interfaces and mutual fertilization of algebraic geometry and string theory, especially [[Mirror symmetry (string theory)|mirror symmetry]].

In 1992–1993, 1996–1997 and 2000 he was at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. In 1995 he was a visiting professor at [[Cornell University]], in 2005 at the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics]], and in 2006 a research professor at [[Mathematical Sciences Research Institute|MSRI]].

In 2015 he became a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], in 2013 a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]], in 2005 a Senior Scholar at the [[Clay Mathematics Institute]] and in 2005–2006 a [[Guggenheim Fellow]].

He is a co-editor of selected works of his thesis supervisor [[Phillip Griffiths]].

Morrison was an [[list of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers|invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Zürich in 1994 (''Mirror Symmetry and Moduli Spaces of Superconformal Field Theories'').

* ''Quantum field theory, supersymmetry, and enumerative geometry''. Freed, Daniel S. and Morrison, David R. and [[Isadore Singer|Singer, Isadore]] editors. IAS/Park City Mathematics Series, Vol. 11. American Mathematical Society Providence, RI viii+285. Papers from the Graduate Summer School of the IAS/Park City Mathematics Institute held in Princeton, NJ, 2001. (2006)
* ''Quantum fields and strings: a course for mathematicians''. Vol. 1, 2. Material from the Special Year on Quantum Field Theory held at the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, NJ, 1996–1997. Edited by [[Pierre Deligne]], [[Pavel Etingof]], Daniel S. Freed, [[Lisa C. Jeffrey]], [[David Kazhdan]], [[John Morgan (mathematician)|John W. Morgan]], David R. Morrison and [[Edward Witten]]. American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI; Institute for Advanced Study (IAS), Princeton, NJ, 1999. Vol. 1: xxii+723 pp.; Vol. 2: pp. i--xxiv and 727–1501. {{ISBN|0-8218-1198-3}}, 81-06 (81T30 81Txx)
* [https://arxiv.org/abs/arXiv:alg-geom/9202004 ''Mirror symmetry and rational curves on quintic threefolds: A guide for mathematicians''], J. Amer. Math. Soc. 6, 1993, 223–247, {{MR|1179538}}
* [https://arxiv.org/abs/arXiv:alg-geom/9609021 ''Mathematical aspects of mirror symmetry''], in [[János Kollár]] (ed.) ''Complex Algebraic Geometry'', IAS/Park City Math. Series, Vol. 3, 1997, pp.&nbsp;265–340.
* [https://arxiv.org/abs/arXiv:math.AG/0007090 ''Mathematical Aspects of Mirror Symmetry''], in [[Björn Engquist]], [[Wilfried Schmid]] ''Mathematics Unlimited'', Springer Verlag 2001, Arxiv.org
